question: What is the key difference between SAST and DAST?

options.text: SAST is used in production, DAST — only in development
options.explanation: The opposite. SAST runs in CI on every MR. DAST requires a running application and is often used with staging/review environments.

options.text: SAST is faster, DAST — slower
options.explanation: Speed is a consequence, not the essence. SAST is faster precisely because it does not run the application, but this is not the main difference.

options.text: SAST analyzes source code without running it, DAST attacks a running application
options.explanation: Correct. SAST — static code analysis (like a proofreader reading a manuscript). DAST — dynamic testing of a live application (like a hacker trying attacks in real time).

options.text: SAST only finds SQL injections, DAST — XSS vulnerabilities
options.explanation: Both tools can find both types of vulnerabilities. The difference is not in the vulnerability types but in the analysis method.

question: You add SAST to the pipeline via the GitLab template. What happens if the repository has both Python and JavaScript code?

options.text: GitLab will launch only one analyzer — for the language with the most files
options.explanation: GitLab launches analyzers for all detected languages, not just the predominant one.

options.text: The template will only launch semgrep — a universal analyzer for all languages
options.explanation: The template launches multiple specialized analyzers, not just semgrep. Semgrep is one option, but not the only one.

options.text: GitLab will automatically detect both languages and run bandit (Python) and eslint (JavaScript) in parallel
options.explanation: Exactly. GitLab scans the repository, detects languages, and launches the corresponding analyzers. This is one of the main conveniences of the template approach.

options.text: You need to explicitly specify the language in the SAST_ANALYZER variable — otherwise there will be an error
options.explanation: Explicit specification is not required. GitLab automatically detects languages.

question: How does Dependency Scanning differ from Container Scanning?

options.text: Both tools do the same thing, Container Scanning just comes with a paid plan
options.explanation: The tools analyze fundamentally different components: code vs. image. This is not a pricing question.

options.text: Dependency Scanning is only for Python, Container Scanning — for Node.js
options.explanation: Dependency Scanning supports all major package managers. Container Scanning works with any Docker image regardless of the application language.

options.text: Dependency Scanning is faster and cheaper, Container Scanning is more accurate
options.explanation: Comparison by speed/accuracy does not capture the essence. The tools check different layers of the application.

options.text: Dependency Scanning checks code dependencies (npm, pip), Container Scanning — OS packages in the Docker image
options.explanation: Correct. Dependency Scanning works with lock files (package-lock.json, requirements.txt). Container Scanning analyzes installed operating system packages inside the image — OpenSSL, libc, etc.

question: A developer committed an AWS key and immediately removed it in the next commit. Did Secret Detection find it?

options.text: No — Secret Detection only checks the current state of files
options.explanation: This is a common misconception. Secret Detection (e.g., gitleaks) analyzes git history, not just current files.

options.text: Yes — Secret Detection analyzes git history and will find the key in the previous commit
options.explanation: Correct. Tools like gitleaks scan the entire git history. A secret removed in a subsequent commit remains in history forever unless git rebase/rewrite is performed.

options.text: Depends on configuration — by default only the current commit
options.explanation: By default, gitleaks checks changes in the commit, but full history scanning can be configured. The GitLab template is configured to analyze the MR delta.

options.text: Secret Detection cannot check git history — only the filesystem
options.explanation: gitleaks is specifically designed for git history analysis. This is its primary function.

question: Why is the --ignore-unfixed flag important in Container Scanning?

options.text: It disables OS package checks and leaves only application checks
options.explanation: The flag does not change the scanning scope. It only affects whether to show vulnerabilities for which no fix exists.

options.text: It skips vulnerabilities for which there is no patch — otherwise the report is flooded with unfixed issues
options.explanation: Correct. Without this flag, the report contains hundreds of vulnerabilities in the base image for which maintainers have not yet released a patch. The developer cannot do anything about them right now — this is noise.

options.text: It speeds up scanning by skipping fixed vulnerabilities
options.explanation: The flag affects result filtering, not speed. It skips vulnerabilities without a patch.

options.text: It ignores vulnerabilities rated below HIGH
options.explanation: Filtering by severity uses the --severity flag. --ignore-unfixed filters by patch status, not by criticality.

question: A team is just starting to implement security scanning. Everything is configured with allow_failure: false. What happened the next day?

options.text: All MRs are blocked due to dependency vulnerabilities — development has stopped
options.explanation: This is exactly what happens. A typical project immediately has dozens of vulnerabilities, many of which are false positives or known acceptable risks. The correct approach: start with allow_failure: true, review results, gradually tighten.

options.text: The pipeline became much more secure — all vulnerabilities are blocked
options.explanation: Theoretically correct, but in practice without gradual implementation the team will start bypassing or disabling security jobs.

options.text: GitLab automatically created issues for each vulnerability
options.explanation: GitLab can create issues automatically, but this is configured separately. By default, vulnerabilities only appear in the Security Dashboard.

options.text: Nothing changed — allow_failure: false does not affect the result, only the UI appearance
options.explanation: allow_failure: false is exactly what blocks the MR when a job fails. This is a critically important setting.

question: Which base Docker image creates the smallest attack surface?

options.text: node:18 — the official image with proper security settings
options.explanation: node:18 is based on Debian and contains many unnecessary packages. node:18-alpine or distroless are significantly better from a security standpoint.

options.text: gcr.io/distroless/nodejs18 — runtime only, no shell or system utilities
options.explanation: Distroless contains a minimal set: only application runtime dependencies. No bash, no apt, no curl — nothing to attack. Container Scanning will find minimal vulnerabilities.

options.text: scratch — a completely empty image
options.explanation: scratch is indeed minimal, but requires a statically compiled binary. It does not work for Node.js/Python/Java — there is no runtime.

options.text: ubuntu:22.04 — stable, well maintained
options.explanation: Ubuntu contains hundreds of packages, most of which are not needed by the application. More packages — more potential vulnerabilities.

question: Where in the pipeline should DAST be placed?

options.text: In parallel with SAST — both tools are independent
options.explanation: SAST does not require a running application and runs in parallel with tests. DAST requires one — therefore they cannot be parallel at the same stage.

options.text: In a separate scheduled pipeline — once a day on a schedule
options.explanation: A scheduled pipeline is possible but insufficient. DAST should run on every MR against a review app — otherwise the point of early vulnerability detection is lost.

options.text: After deployment to a staging/review environment — DAST needs a running service
options.explanation: Correct. DAST sends real HTTP requests to the application. Therefore, the application must be running — on a review app or staging. DAST always comes after the deploy stage.

options.text: At the very beginning — to check security before building
options.explanation: DAST requires a working application. It is impossible to run it without deployment.

question: Scanning is configured in the pipeline, but developers ignore the results and continue pushing. What needs to change?

options.text: Send automatic emails for every found vulnerability
options.explanation: Email notifications with high noise will turn into spam and be ignored just like the results in the UI.

options.text: Configure Security Approvals in GitLab — the MR cannot be merged without approval from a Security Champion
options.explanation: Correct. Technical control: Project Settings -> Security -> Merge Request Approvals. Critical vulnerabilities block the merge until approval is obtained. Organizational control: assign a responsible Security Champion.

options.text: Add more tools — the more scanning, the better
options.explanation: The problem is not the number of tools but the processes. Adding more tools will only increase noise.

options.text: Switch all tools to allow_failure: false — let the pipeline fail
options.explanation: Without a configured vulnerability handling process, this will simply block development. The team will find a way to bypass it — for example, disabling scanning altogether.

question: Why is it important to exclude vendor/, node_modules/, and test/ from SAST scanning?

options.text: Vulnerabilities in vendor/ and test fixtures are false positives or someone else's responsibility; noise hides real problems
options.explanation: Correct. Vulnerabilities in vendor/ are the responsibility of Dependency Scanning, not SAST. Test fixtures may contain intentionally insecure code for testing. Hundreds of false positives will hide real problems in your code.

options.text: GitLab requires explicit scanning paths — without exclusions the pipeline will fail with an error
options.explanation: GitLab does not require explicit exclusions. Without them, scanning will simply produce more results, many of which will be irrelevant.

options.text: Exclusion speeds up scanning — SAST does not waste time on extra files
options.explanation: Speed is a bonus, but not the main reason. The main reason is report quality.

options.text: These directories are access-protected and SAST cannot read them
options.explanation: There are no technical restrictions. The problem lies elsewhere — result quality.

question: Your Node.js project uses a library with a critical CVE. Dependency Scanning found it. A patch has not yet been released. What to do?

options.text: Immediately write an issue in the library's repository and wait
options.explanation: Writing an issue is useful, but insufficient as an immediate action. You need to assess risk and decide on temporary measures right now.

options.text: Add the vulnerability to an allowlist and forget about it
options.explanation: Adding without analysis and documentation is bad practice. You need to regularly review accepted risks and monitor for patch availability.

options.text: Assess risk: is the vulnerable functionality vulnerable in your context? Document the accepted risk or find a fork/alternative
options.explanation: The correct process. Not all CVEs are critical in a specific context. For example, a vulnerability in an XML parser is not dangerous if you only parse internal data. GitLab allows marking a vulnerability as 'Accepted Risk' with an explanation.

options.text: Remove the library — better without functionality than with a vulnerability
options.explanation: This is an extreme measure. First, assess the real risk, find alternatives, or apply temporary measures.

question: A developer accidentally committed a .env file with real passwords. Secret Detection triggered. What actions are needed URGENTLY?

options.text: Make the repository private — so no one can see the history
options.explanation: This is not a solution. First, someone with access may have already copied the secret. Second, it does not eliminate the problem — the secret is still in history.

options.text: Remove the .env file in the next commit and add it to .gitignore
options.explanation: Insufficient. The file will remain in git history. Secrets must be rotated immediately — they are compromised.

options.text: Ask the GitLab administrator to delete the specific commit
options.explanation: Deleting the commit helps but is not enough — secrets need to be rotated. Moreover, if the repository was mirrored or cloned by someone, the secret has already leaked.

options.text: Rotate (change) all compromised secrets immediately, then clean git history via rebase/filter-branch
options.explanation: The correct sequence. First rotate — an attacker may have already taken the secrets. Then clean history. If the repository is public, consider the secrets compromised from the moment of push.

question: How does zap-baseline.py differ from zap-full-scan.py in the CI/CD context?

options.text: baseline — for development, full-scan — for production environment
options.explanation: The difference is not in the environment but in the scanning type. Both can be used in CI, but with different consequences.

options.text: Both are identical in functionality, the difference is only in execution time
options.explanation: The functionality differs fundamentally: passive vs. active. This is not a speed question.

options.text: baseline only checks headers, full-scan — the entire application
options.explanation: baseline checks more than just headers. It analyzes the application structure, just without active attacks.

options.text: baseline — passive scanning (only observes), full-scan — active (tries attacks, can modify data)
options.explanation: Exactly. baseline does not attack — it analyzes traffic and configuration. full-scan actively tries SQL injections, XSS, and other attacks, which can corrupt database data. In CI, baseline is almost always used.

question: GitLab provides the templates Security/SAST.gitlab-ci.yml and Security/Dependency-Scanning.gitlab-ci.yml. What do you need to write to use both?

options.text: extends: [Security/SAST.gitlab-ci.yml, Security/Dependency-Scanning.gitlab-ci.yml]
options.explanation: extends is used for inheriting job configuration, not for including external files. For including templates — only include.

options.text: include with an array of two elements: - template: Security/SAST.gitlab-ci.yml and - template: Security/Dependency-Scanning.gitlab-ci.yml
options.explanation: Correct. include accepts a list, each element is a separate template. GitLab merges all included configs into one pipeline.

options.text: include: template: Security/SAST.gitlab-ci.yml — one include for all security templates
options.explanation: One include connects only one template. For multiple templates, you need a list.

options.text: Write two separate include: keys — one for each template
options.explanation: Two separate include: keys will overwrite each other — YAML does not allow duplicate keys.

question: A team configured Dependency Scanning with DS_MAX_SEVERITY: high. A found vulnerability has severity MEDIUM. Will the pipeline fail?

options.text: GitLab will ask the maintainer — whether to block MEDIUM
options.explanation: There is no interactive query. Behavior is fully determined by the DS_MAX_SEVERITY configuration.

options.text: Yes — high includes medium, since medium is lower in criticality
options.explanation: DS_MAX_SEVERITY: high means 'stop on HIGH and CRITICAL'. MEDIUM is not included in this threshold.

options.text: Depends on allow_failure — if true, the pipeline will not fail regardless of severity
options.explanation: allow_failure affects the behavior when a job fails in general, but DS_MAX_SEVERITY is the internal logic of the scanning tool itself.

options.text: No — DS_MAX_SEVERITY: high means 'block only HIGH and CRITICAL', MEDIUM is allowed through
options.explanation: Correct. The variable sets the minimum severity level for blocking. HIGH blocks HIGH and CRITICAL. MEDIUM will be displayed in the report but will not stop the pipeline.
